title: The imperative: giving directions
topic: affirmative imperative with tú and usted; irregular imperatives
why: Until now, you gave directions using the present; now you finally discover the affirmative imperative, for tú (habla, sigue, and the eight irregular ones ven, ve, sal, haz, di, pon, ten, sé) and for usted (siga, gire, vaya, venga, haga). With attached pronouns (siéntate, cógelo), you can give directions, a recipe or instructions, whether traveling or at home.

The imperative with tú

In English, a command is just the bare verb (“speak”, “turn”), whoever you're talking to. Spanish has different forms for tú and usted. Good news: for tú, the regular affirmative imperative is identical to the third person singular of the present, the él form. So you already know almost all the forms, including those of stem-changing verbs.

InfinitivePresent (él)Imperative (tú)Example
hablarhablahablaHabla despacio, por favor.
girargiragiraGira a la derecha.
cruzarcruzacruzaCruza la plaza.
cogercogecogeCoge la primera calle.
seguirsiguesigueSigue todo recto.
volvervuelvevuelveVuelve pronto.
cerrarcierracierraCierra la puerta.

Eight irregular imperatives

Eight very common verbs have a short form, often just one syllable. They're so frequent that you'll learn them quickly.

venirirsalirhacerdecirponertenerser
venvesalhazdipontensé
comegogo out, leavedo, makesay, tellputhave, holdbe
Ven aquí, pon la mesa y haz la ensalada, por favor.Come here, set the table and make the salad, please.

Sé (be) has an accent, like sé (I know): Sé bueno (be good). For vosotros, the imperative has another form (hablad, venid): you'll see it later.

", "

The imperative with usted

To address someone formally, Spanish borrows a form of the subjunctive, a mood English barely uses and that you'll study in detail later. For now, just learn it as the usted imperative. The principle: take the yo form of the present, drop the -o and “swap” the vowel: -ar → -e, -er / -ir → -a.

InfinitivePresent (yo)Imperative (usted)
hablarhablohable
girargirogire
comercomocoma
subirsubosuba
seguirsigosiga
volvervuelvovuelva
cogercojocoja
venirvengovenga
hacerhagohaga
tenertengotenga
ponerpongoponga
salirsalgosalga
decirdigodiga
irvoyvaya (irregular)

The spelling adapts, just like in llegué, busqué, empecé: cruzar → cruce, llegar → llegue, buscar → busque.

Perdone, ¿para ir a la estación? — Siga todo recto, cruce la plaza y gire a la izquierda.Excuse me, how do I get to the station? — Go straight ahead, cross the square and turn left.

You were already using this imperative without knowing it: perdone (excuse me) comes from perdonar. For several people addressed formally (ustedes), just add -n: sigan, giren, vengan.

", "

Attached pronouns: siéntate, levántese, cógelo

In the affirmative imperative, pronouns don't go in front of the verb: they attach to the end, making a single word. To keep the stress in the same place, you often add a written accent.

InfinitiveTúUstedEnglish
sentarsesiéntatesiéntesesit down
levantarselevántatelevánteseget up, stand up
coger (el billete)cógelocójalotake it
abrir (la puerta)ábrelaábralaopen it
ponerse (el abrigo)pontepóngaseput on (your coat)

In the kitchen: a recipe

Pela las patatas y córtalas en trozos pequeños. Pon aceite en la sartén, fríe las patatas y añade los huevos batidos.Peel the potatoes and cut them into small pieces. Put oil in the frying pan, fry the potatoes and add the beaten eggs.

The negative: just for recognizing

Careful: in the negative, the imperative changes completely (no cruces, no gire). You'll study it later; for now, just learn to recognize it: No gire a la izquierda = “Don't turn left”.

The pronoun attaches to the imperative, but stays in front of conjugated forms: Lo coges (you take it) / Cógelo (take it). In a command, the pronoun comes after the verb, just like “take it” in English; the difference is that Spanish writes it as one word.
